newsitem.title: PERU: Misplaced tape may have caused air crash, Peru says.
newsitem.headline: Misplaced tape may have caused air crash, Peru says.

text.p: Adhesive tape covering altitude and speed sensors may have caused the air crash last month of a Boeing 757-200 airliner that killed all 70 on board, Peru's Transport Ministry said on Tuesday.

The obstruction of these instruments by maintenance workers "could explain the erroneous and confused information about height and speed that was received by the pilots after takeoff," the ministry said in a statement.

The tape, covering sensors used to measure atmospheric pressure, was found in the plane's main body in the Pacific Ocean where it crashed on Oct. 2 soon after taking off for Santiago, Chile, from Lima in heavy fog.

"We have observed that these (sensors) are covered with adhesive tape, a normal procedure in the maintenance of planes during polishing," the ministry said, without explaining why the tape was not removed before flight.

Previously, the Peruvian government had pinned the blame for the accident on technical faults that made the computers aboard the plane "go crazy," leaving the pilot, Eric Schreiber, without instruments as he struggled to return to Lima.

"We've lost the basic instruments, both for height and for speed ... Where am I? Over land or sea?" Schreiber said during a dramatic, 29-minute dialogue with Lima air traffic control, before his jet plunged into the sea in the middle of the night.

An official investigating team from Aeroperu, Boeing, engine maker Pratt & Whitney, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transporation Safety Board has so far reserved judgment on the causes of the crash.
A Boeing spokeswoman in Seattle said earlier on Tuesday information on causes was merely "speculation" until authorities issued final reports.

Rescue workers had by the weekend recovered the corpses of 55 victims from the crash, and continued this week to look for the remaining 15, according to Aeroperu, the local airline that owned the plane.
The 70 dead came from Chile, Peru, Mexico, Ecuador, the United States, Italy, Great Britain, New Zealand, Spain, Colombia and Venezuela.

The accident, one of the worst in Peru's aviation history, came seven months after a Boeing 737 belonging to local Faucett airline crashed and killed all 123 people on board near Peru's second city, Arequipa.
It was also the first of three major air disasters in South America last month.

Last week, a Brazilian commercial jet crashed in a residential area of Sao Paulo, killing all 96 on board. One week earlier a Boeing 707 cargo plane burst into flames and crashed into a densely populated poor district of the port of Manta in southeast Ecuador, killing 25 and injuring 60.
